\chapter{The Face on the Page}
\label{ch:bn-face-on-the-page}
\hlchaptermodality{21}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read \bn{চোখ}, \bn{নাক}, \bn{মুখ} and \bn{হৃদয়} off the page, hear which of them ends in breath and which in silence, and write the one sign the fourth of them needed.}

Heart is read last because it is the only one of the four words that needed a new sign, and the chapter ends with all four read back — thirteen pieces, one of them bought today.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[chokh]{\bn{চোখ} — eye, read}

\label{lesson:BN-W04-chokh-read}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\bn{ভাই}}. Then write \textbf{\bn{চ}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{চ}} + \textbf{\bn{ো}} + \textbf{\bn{খ}} $\to$ \textbf{\bn{চোখ}}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\bn{চ}} wrapped in \textbf{\bn{ো}} — \emph{cho}
  \item \textbf{\bn{খ}} — the breathy \emph{k}, and at the end of a word the breath is what a listener actually hears
\end{itemize}

\textbf{chokh} — \emph{eye.} Three pieces, no new shapes, and it is the first word of the chapter on the face.

Look at the \textbf{\bn{ো}} again. It is the one vowel sign that arrives in two halves, one on each side of its consonant, and the eye has to take the whole cluster in at once rather than reading left to right through it. That is a small demonstration of something true of the whole script: \textbf{a Bengali syllable is a unit on the page, not a sequence.} The letters inside it may be written before, after, above or below each other, and the reader assembles the syllable, not the strokes.

It is worth noticing what this word is asking of you at the moment you read it. The organ named is the one doing the reading.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \bn{চোখ}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{চোখ}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{চ} \bn{ছ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{chokh}, letting the breath out at the end
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many pieces in \textbf{\bn{চোখ}}? (\textbf{Three}.) Which sign sits on both sides of its consonant? (\textbf{\bn{ো}}.) And how many of the three shapes were new today? (\textbf{None}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nāk]{\bn{নাক} — nose, read}

\label{lesson:BN-W04-nak-read}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\bn{চোখ}}. Then write \textbf{\bn{ক}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{ন}} + \textbf{\bn{া}} + \textbf{\bn{ক}} $\to$ \textbf{\bn{নাক}}
\end{quote}

\textbf{nāk} — \emph{nose.} Every piece of this word came out of the chapter that taught you to read the greeting, several thousand words ago. Nothing has been added since, and nothing needed to be.

Two things about the last letter. \textbf{\bn{ক}} ends the word, so its inherent \textbf{ô} is gone — the mouth closes and stops, with no vowel after it. And the closure is \textbf{clean}: no breath escapes, which is the whole difference between this letter and the \textbf{\bn{খ}} that ended \textbf{\bn{চোখ}} a moment ago. Read the two words one after the other and the contrast is unmissable:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{চোখ}} — ends in air \textbf{\bn{নাক}} — ends in silence
\end{quote}

That pair is the best short demonstration of aspiration this book can offer, because both words are things you can point at on your own face.

Say it and mean it. \textbf{\bn{নাক}} is a plain, unglamorous, everyday word, and being able to read one of those off the page without help is a better measure of progress than being able to read a beautiful one.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \bn{নাক}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \bn{চোখ} \bn{নাক}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{নাক}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{ক} \bn{খ} \bn{গ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{chokh}, then \emph{nāk} — air, then silence
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What happens to \textbf{\bn{ক}}'s inherent vowel at the end of \textbf{\bn{নাক}}? (\textbf{It is gone}.) Which of \textbf{\bn{চোখ}} and \textbf{\bn{নাক}} ends in breath? (\textbf{\bn{চোখ}}.) And which chapter's letters is \textbf{\bn{নাক}} built from? (\textbf{The first script chapter's}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mukh]{\bn{মুখ} — mouth, read}

\label{lesson:BN-W03-mukh-read}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\bn{খ}}, then write \textbf{\bn{ু}} underneath it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{ম}} + \textbf{\bn{ু}} + \textbf{\bn{খ}} $\to$ \textbf{\bn{মুখ}}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\bn{ম}} with \textbf{\bn{ু}} hanging under it — \emph{mu}
  \item \textbf{\bn{খ}} — the breathy \emph{k}, and at the end of a word its inherent vowel is gone, so what is left is the closure and the puff
\end{itemize}

\textbf{mukh} — \emph{mouth}, from the chapter on the face. A tatsama: kept whole out of Sanskrit rather than worn down on the way.

The end of this word is where a new reader loses the breath. English speakers finishing a word on \emph{k} stop the air dead; Bengali lets it out. Say \emph{mu}, close on the back of the tongue, and then open. If the last thing a listener hears is air, it was right.

There is a smaller thing worth seeing on the page. Three letters, one sign, and the sign is the only mark below the head-line in the whole word. A Bengali word's information is not spread evenly — most of it rides on the band, and the occasional piece that drops below is doing work the eye must not skip.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \bn{মুখ}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \bn{ভালো}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{মুখ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What happens to the breath at the end of \textbf{\bn{মুখ}}? (It \textbf{comes out} — the letter is the breathy one.) And where is the only mark below the head-line? (Under the \textbf{first} letter.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-ri]{\bn{ৃ} — the vowel that used to be an \emph{r}}

\label{lesson:BN-W04-ri-matra}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\bn{মুখ}}. Then write \textbf{\bn{ু}} and say which side of the head-line it hangs on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\bn{ৃ}
\end{quote}

A hook hanging under its consonant, in the same country as \textbf{\bn{ু}}. It is a \textbf{vowel sign}, and it says \textbf{ri}.

The reason it is filed with the vowels and not with \textbf{\bn{র}} is a piece of history worth two minutes. Sanskrit had a sound that behaved like a vowel and was made like an \emph{r}: a syllable you could build a word around with no other vowel in it at all. English does this without noticing — the second syllable of \emph{butter} has no vowel letter doing any work, only the \emph{r}. Sanskrit wrote that syllable, and counted it among its vowels.

Bengali kept the sign and gave up the sound. What a Bengali reader says today is plain \textbf{ri}. So the mark is a vowel that no longer sounds like the thing it is named after, and its position in the alphabet is a fossil.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{হ}} + \textbf{\bn{ৃ}} $\to$ \textbf{\bn{হৃ}}
\end{quote}

Look at where it goes and what it does to the letter above it. On \textbf{\bn{হ}} the hook is tucked into the letter's own tail, which is why this combination looks like a single new shape rather than a letter plus a mark. That is normal for this sign and it is the main difficulty it presents: \textbf{\bn{ৃ}} is a mark that hides.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{ৃ}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{হৃ}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{ু} then \bn{ৃ} — both below the line
  \item \emph{Read it:} \bn{নাক}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \textbf{\bn{ৃ}} a consonant or a vowel sign? (\textbf{A vowel sign}.) What does it say in Bengali today? (\emph{\textbf{ri}}.) And is it the letter \textbf{\bn{র}}? (\textbf{No} — a different mark, in a different place.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hridoy]{\bn{হৃদয়} — heart, and the face read whole}

\label{lesson:BN-W04-hridoy-read}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\bn{হৃ}}. Then write \textbf{\bn{দ}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{হ}} + \textbf{\bn{ৃ}} + \textbf{\bn{দ}} + \textbf{\bn{য়}} $\to$ \textbf{\bn{হৃদয়}}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\bn{হৃ}} — the breath with the hidden hook under it, \emph{hri}
  \item \textbf{\bn{দ}} — the dental \emph{d}, carrying its inherent \textbf{ô}
  \item \textbf{\bn{য়}} — the dotted glide, closing the word
\end{itemize}

\textbf{hridoy} — \emph{heart.} Four pieces, and three of the four are things this book bought for other words entirely: the \textbf{\bn{দ}} came from milk, the \textbf{\bn{য়}} came from the verb of being, and only the hook was bought for this word alone.

That is the ordinary economy of a syllabary, and it is why a reader's progress accelerates. The first word cost nine lessons. This one cost one.

The spelling is also a small piece of evidence. \textbf{\bn{হৃদয়}} is a \textbf{tatsama} — a word Bengali took out of Sanskrit whole rather than wearing it down over centuries — and you can see that in the letters. A worn-down word would have lost this hook long ago, the way \textbf{\bn{ভাই}} lost the one its Sanskrit ancestor had. Spelling is where a language keeps its receipts.

Now the whole chapter, off the page:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{চোখ}} · \textbf{\bn{নাক}} · \textbf{\bn{মুখ}} · \textbf{\bn{হৃদয়}}
\end{quote}

Four words, thirteen pieces, one new sign between them.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \bn{হৃদয়}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \bn{চোখ} \bn{নাক} \bn{মুখ} \bn{হৃদয়}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{হৃদয়}
  \item \emph{Say it:} all four, pointing at each
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many pieces in \textbf{\bn{হৃদয়}}? (\textbf{Four}.) How many of them were bought for this word? (\textbf{One} — the hook.) Which letter is wearing a dot? (\textbf{\bn{য়}}.) And name the four words of this chapter in Bengali. (\textbf{\bn{চোখ}, \bn{নাক}, \bn{মুখ}, \bn{হৃদয়}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
